learning.title: A screen that matches its design can still be unreadable: say each thing once, and design the whole page
learning.trigger: Designing, building, reviewing or approving any screen in apps/web or packages/ui, especially a new section, banner, chip or card on a page that already has content, or a visual review that passes because the stills match the design.
learning.mistake: Pull requests 885 (task page preview card) and 886 (task Delivery section) passed design, QA and tests and were rejected by the owner on sight: "very busy-looking", "I couldn't tell you what this screen's actually doing", "terrible use of white space", "too much information", and "a consistent trend with all of these pages". The screens were built in slices. Each slice added its own section, banner or chip, and each was checked only against its own design. The result: one fact shown three times (try 2 of 2 in a banner, a section and a row; older commit as a badge, a warning box and a commit line); two commit ids beside the answer; four sections each with an icon, an info mark, a summary line and a chip; stacked empty-state lines ("No steps have been recorded", "No artifacts to show", "Provider usage: unknown"); four faded run buttons that could not apply to the current state. Every gate asked "does it match the design and the acceptance criteria"; none asked "can a stranger say what this screen is doing".
learning.rule: Give every screen one sentence it answers (for example, "Is my change ready, and what is it waiting for?"), one primary action, and at most one banner. Write the sentence at the top of the design before drawing anything.

Say each fact once. If a state shows in a banner, do not repeat it in a section summary, a chip and a line. Count the facts on the screen; a fact shown twice is a defect even when the design asked for it.

Lead with what needs attention. Fold passed or settled items into a count, put history and technical detail (commit ids, exit codes, attempt logs) behind a details link, and hide any part with nothing to show instead of printing "No X" or "Y: unknown". Do not show controls that cannot apply to the current state.

Design the whole page, not the new piece. When a page is already dense, the next slice is a change to the page's design, owned by design-ux, before any code. A slice that adds a section to a dense page without that is the mistake above.

Review by the five-second test. From the screenshot alone, write one sentence saying what the screen is doing and what the person does next. If you cannot, the screen fails, whatever the design says. Cover everything except the headline and the primary action: the screen should still make sense.

verification.requirement: The UX design comment opens with the one sentence the screen answers, its single primary action, and each fact named once.
The QA visual review has a Clarity result per screen: the one-sentence description, and any repeated facts, empty-state lines, extra banners or inapplicable controls listed for removal.
design-ux sign-off records the cover test, the repeated-fact count and the number of banners.
A reviewer treats a state shown more than once on a screen as a medium finding, and a missing Clarity result as high.

learning.boundary: Repetition that serves a different reader is fine: a screen-reader-only status, a row's state also in its accessible name, a short summary above a table that the table's rows detail. A dense screen is also right when density is the job (a log, a diff, a data table the person scans). The rule is that the headline and the action must still be obvious, and that nothing is said twice without a reason.
